title: 6 Best On Call Schedule Generators for Hospital Teams
description: Six ways to build an on-call schedule for a hospital team, from simple rotations to GME programs with ACGME rules and linked block, call and clinic.
content:
Summary

  • A published study of one residency's rebuilt call schedule found residents' perceived fairness rose from 43% to 95%.
  • This article ranks scheduling tools by complexity tolerance, from simple roster publishing to solutions for high-rule GME programs, helping you find the right fit for your needs.
  • GME scheduling is a rules problem, not a simple calendar task, with interdependent Block, Call and Clinic schedules and ACGME requirements to build to.
  • For programs that lose their scheduler every July when the chief changes, a managed service like Scheduling Wizard delivers finished schedules built to your requirements without requiring staff to learn new software.

If you're a chief resident, you already know the drill. Every year, someone inherits the "BIG Spreadsheet", a sprawling Excel file that represents months of accumulated scheduling logic, workarounds, and institutional memory. And every year, that knowledge walks out the door at graduation.

Chief residents in online discussions often end up back where they started; as one put it, "Nothing was able to deliver quite like Excel."

There's also healthy skepticism about AI-powered solutions; as one chief put it, AI "won't do a good job yet." That's a fair concern, and it applies to a lot of generic automation tools thrown at scheduling problems that are hard. Coordinating 80 residents across two hospitals, balancing vacation requests, elective rotations, graduation requirements, seniority rules, and strict ACGME duty hour rules is a rules problem, not a calendar management task.

This article is ranked differently from most on call schedule generator roundups. Instead of listing tools alphabetically or by popularity, we've ordered them by who builds the schedule, and noted how much complexity each can take, from simple daily rosters all the way to high-rule GME programs. Find where your team sits on that range and start there.

You'll encounter two broad categories:

  • Self-service software: You learn the platform, input the rules, and manage the process.
  • Managed services: You submit your rules and receive a finished schedule, no software to learn.

A note before the list: we are Scheduling Wizard. We build physician schedules as a service, so we have included ourselves below and you should read our entry with that in mind. The order here is by one thing only, who actually builds the schedule, which is why a service comes first and the spreadsheet second; the software and the platforms you publish through follow. Rank by cost, or by how good the mobile app is, and the order changes. We have described the other tools as their own users and documentation describe them.

Why Getting Scheduling Right Actually Matters

For residents specifically, a study published in Neurosurgery found that a rebuilt call schedule increased the perceived fairness of call schedules from 43% to 95%.

The 6 Options, Ordered by Who Builds the Schedule

1. Scheduling Wizard: Best for Programs With Complicated Rules

Complexity Tier: Highest | Model: Managed Service | ACGME Support: Built in

Scheduling Wizard is first because it is the one option here where someone else builds the schedule and hands it back finished.

Programs submit their residents, rotations, and full rule set, vacation requests, conference days, clinic requirements, seniority rules (e.g., "1 senior, 1 medium, and 2 novice members per call slot"), maximum hours, subspecialty-specific ACGME rules, and Scheduling Wizard's team returns the finished block, clinic, call and attending schedules. There is nothing to learn or configure, and the schedule is checked before you see it.

Why this matters for GME programs specifically:

In residency scheduling the ACGME rules sit under everything else. We treat the ACGME requirements as rules of the build from the start, not a flag raised after a violation is already baked into the schedule. Anything your specialty's Review Committee adds goes in the same way, alongside your local rules.

The output format is deliberate: Excel or Google Sheets, or a custom live view, ready for whatever platform the program already uses day to day. This addresses the widely-shared frustration that "nothing was able to deliver quite like Excel", because the output is Excel, without your team doing the build.

The other difference is continuity. Every year when chief residents graduate, scheduling knowledge resets. Scheduling Wizard retains a program's rules, preferences and requests across annual rotations. New chiefs don't start from zero.

Currently serving 20+ hospitals and practices and 30+ departments, Scheduling Wizard is a YC-backed managed service started on the GME scheduling problem, not adapted from a general workforce scheduling tool.

Key differentiators:

  • Done-for-you: no software to learn or operate
  • Built to the ACGME requirements you tell us apply
  • Handles Block, Clinic, Call, and Attending schedules simultaneously
  • Resolves cross-schedule dependencies in the build
  • Institutional knowledge preserved year over year
  • Delivered as Excel, Google Sheets or a custom live view, ready for whatever platform you publish through

What you get: the finished call schedule in the format your program asks for, Excel or Google Sheets, and a custom live view we build for you if you want one. Major redrafts are part of the engagement rather than an extra: when someone goes on leave, changes rotation or leaves mid-year, we rebuild around the gap. For the specifics, see our page on on-call schedule building. We build to your rules and requests, however granular, with the ACGME requirements among them.

2. Excel / Google Sheets

Complexity Tier: Any, with enough hours | Model: Manual | ACGME Support: None

A spreadsheet is second, not last. There is no rule it cannot hold, because the modeling happens in a person's head rather than in a configuration screen. That is a real advantage for programs with unusual local rules.

What limits it is arithmetic and time. Keeping a four-week rolling average correct across thirty residents, while every change moves three other schedules, is the part that does not scale. The file holds the answer but not the reasoning, so it cannot be inherited.

3. Lightning Bolt: Best for Rule-Based Automation with Manual Control

Complexity Tier: High | Model: Self-Service | ACGME Support: Good (rule-based)

Lightning Bolt is one of the more sophisticated self-service on call schedule generators on the market. It uses a rule-based automation engine to generate schedule suggestions based on preferences and rules you define, making it a meaningful step up from pure manual scheduling.

The appeal is clear: you input your team's rules (coverage requirements, time-off preferences, fairness targets), and the system auto-generates a starting point. The platform also tracks scheduling tallies to keep call distribution equitable over time.

The tradeoff is the learning curve. To get value out of Lightning Bolt, someone on your team needs to become a capable user of the platform, correctly configure all rules, and manually review the output for edge cases and conflicts. For a rotating chief resident inheriting a new program, that ramp-up time is a real cost. For GME programs where Block, Call and Clinic requirements all depend on each other, expect time each cycle reviewing and adjusting the output.

For departments with dedicated administrative staff who can own the system long-term, Lightning Bolt offers genuine automation benefits and good reporting.

Key strengths:

  • Automated schedule generation from user-defined rules
  • Provider preference integration
  • Workload balancing and fairness tracking
  • Solid for general physician scheduling and simpler residency programs

Limitation: Does not remove the operator burden; someone still has to learn, configure, and manage the platform, and resolve the conflicts it surfaces.

4. QGenda: Best for Enterprise Standardization Across Large Systems

Complexity Tier: High | Model: Self-Service | ACGME Support: Fair (violation flagging)

QGenda is a well-known name in healthcare workforce management, and for large health systems looking to standardize scheduling across multiple departments, it's a logical choice. It extends beyond scheduling into credentialing, time tracking, and provider data management, making it a genuine enterprise platform rather than a point solution.

It is a substantial platform, and it is usually run by an administrator who owns it full time. For chief residents on one-year terms, that setup and upkeep is a lot to take on.

On the ACGME rules, what the platform does depends on how your team configures it, and your team reviews and resolves whatever it raises.

Many programs we work with keep QGenda or a tool like it: we build the schedule, and residents keep reading it where they do now.

Key strengths:

  • Enterprise-grade centralized scheduling hub
  • Advanced analytics and reporting
  • Integrates with credentialing and payroll systems
  • Strong fit for health systems with dedicated scheduling administrators

Consider: setup and an experienced operator on your side.

5. TigerConnect Physician Scheduling: Best for Communication-First Teams

Complexity Tier: Low to Moderate | Model: Self-Service | ACGME Support: Fair

TigerConnect's physician scheduling module is built into its broader clinical communication platform, which is its primary value proposition. If your hospital already uses TigerConnect for secure messaging, having scheduling live in the same environment reduces app-switching and keeps on-call information accessible alongside the communication tools clinicians already use daily.

The scheduling functionality includes some rule-based capabilities and a mobile-first design, making it accessible for departments that need a straightforward, integrated solution rather than a dedicated scheduling system.

It tends to suit general physician groups, hospitalists, or urgent care teams where scheduling patterns are more predictable and rotations less intertwined.

Key strengths:

  • HIPAA-compliant secure messaging integrated with scheduling
  • Mobile-first, easy access for on-call providers
  • Reduces app-switching for teams already in the TigerConnect ecosystem

Consider: for residency programs with interlocking schedules, compare how much of the build your team would still do.

6. UKG EZCall: Best for Simple Daily On-Call Visibility

Complexity Tier: Low | Model: Self-Service | ACGME Support: Limited

UKG EZCall is built around showing who is on call, right now, across your organization.

For departments where the scheduling itself is relatively simple and repeating, and the main challenge is ensuring the right people can quickly find out who's on call without digging through binders or email chains, EZCall serves that purpose. It supports shift swaps, time-off requests, and real-time visibility from any device.

Building the year's call schedule to the ACGME rules is still work that happens before it.

Key strengths:

  • Clean real-time on-call visibility
  • Simple shift swap and time-off management
  • Works well as a publishing layer for pre-built schedules

Consider: pair it with a separate way of building the schedule if your rules are complex.

How to Choose the Right On-Call Scheduling Tool

The "best" on call schedule generator depends entirely on your team's size, scheduling complexity, and how much administrative capacity you have to operate a tool long-term. Here's a simple framework:

If you run a small urgent care clinic or a single department with simple, repeating rotations: Your primary need is visibility and communication, not complex schedule generation. A self-service tool like UKG EZCall or TigerConnect is likely sufficient. Rotations are predictable, the team is small, and the administrative overhead is manageable.

If you're a large hospital department or health system with dedicated scheduling administrators: You need enterprise power and standardization across multiple service lines. A solid platform like QGenda or Lightning Bolt can work well, provided you have a full-time employee who can own the system, configure rules, and manage it consistently year over year.

If you're a residency program director, fellowship coordinator, or chief resident: Your situation is categorically different. You're dealing with strict ACGME duty hour requirements, subspecialty-specific rules, interdependent Block/Call/Clinic schedules, individual resident preferences, and the annual reset of scheduling knowledge when chiefs graduate. Self-service software places the whole build squarely on whoever happens to be chief that year, a role that's already demanding enough.

A managed service like Scheduling Wizard takes the operator role off the program, builds to the ACGME requirements you tell us apply, and keeps your written-down rules from year to year. Your schedule gets built by our team, who build schedules full time, and lands in your inbox as Excel or Google Sheets, or on a custom live view we build for you. The time your chief residents save goes back to education and patient care.

Which Option Fits Your Team

The on-call scheduling field ranges from simple publishing platforms to sophisticated self-service platforms to fully managed services, and they serve different needs.

For small teams with predictable rotations, a lightweight self-service tool gets the job done. For large systems with dedicated staff, an enterprise platform like QGenda or Lightning Bolt offers the control and standardization worth the investment. For residency and fellowship programs working to the ACGME rules, with interlocking schedules and a chief who changes every year, it is worth considering handing the build over.

That is what Scheduling Wizard does: a finished schedule built to your requirements, with no software for your staff to learn.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the best way to keep a residency schedule inside the ACGME rules?

Put the rules into the schedule while it is built, rather than flagging violations after a schedule exists. Many self-service tools flag, which still leaves a human to resolve the conflicts by hand. A managed service like Scheduling Wizard builds the schedule with the ACGME requirements you tell us apply as rules of the build from the start, and reviews the finished schedule against them before it goes out.

Does Scheduling Wizard replace tools like Amion?

No. It is entirely up to you. We build the schedule either way, and deliver it in the format and structure you want: Excel or Google Sheets, or a custom live view we build for you if that is useful. Many programs keep Amion for day-to-day viewing and upload our schedules straight into it; others use the live view, or both. Whatever works best for your program.

What's the difference between a managed scheduling service and scheduling software?

The key difference is who does the work. With scheduling software, you or your staff operate the tool, configure the rules, and resolve conflicts. With a managed service, you provide your rules and an expert team delivers a finished, ready-to-use schedule. Self-service software requires a significant time investment to learn and operate, whereas a managed service like Scheduling Wizard takes this operator burden off your team.

Why is Excel still so common for residency scheduling?

Excel remains popular because it can hold any rule, including the local and ever-changing ones many GME programs have. While manual scheduling in Excel is incredibly time-consuming and error-prone, it offers total control. Managed services like Scheduling Wizard solve this by doing the build and handing back the familiar spreadsheet.

How can our program maintain scheduling continuity when chief residents graduate?

Write the rules down somewhere that outlasts the chief. Scheduling knowledge gets lost each year because it lives in one person's memory or a complex spreadsheet. A managed service like Scheduling Wizard keeps your program's written-down rules and preferences, so a new chief resident does not start from scratch.
